name: Nilamani Senapati
title: Nilamani Senapati: Keeping a District Within Reach
description: The gazetteer editor whose work helped later readers trace places, people and histories across changing boundaries.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: A place can have one spelling on an official map and another in local use. The preface to the Sundargarh district gazetteer explains how its editors handled that problem: the index would give both spellings, alongside the Odia form. It is a small editorial decision with a lasting purpose. A reader should be able to find the place they know.

Nilamani Senapati appears on the volume’s title page as Chief Editor, a retired member of the Indian Civil Service. Durga Charan Kuanr is named State Editor. Their work belonged to the government’s Gazetteers Unit: the patient business of assembling a district’s past and present into a book that other people could consult.

Sundargarh presented a difficult assignment. Its two former princely states, Gangpur and Bonai, had left no district gazetteers of their own, and the preface describes a shortage of earlier records. Compilers drew on settlement reports, administrative reports and older accounts. The text then underwent scrutiny by a subcommittee and an advisory committee. Senapati’s credit belongs within that collective process, which joined the work of gathering information to the responsibility of checking it.

A gazetteer asks its editors to hold many kinds of knowledge together. A river, an administrative boundary and a remembered kingdom may occupy the same landscape without fitting the same chronology. The value of such a book lies partly in making those connections available to readers who begin with very different questions.

sections.title: A book that survived new boundaries

paragraphs.text: The later Koraput gazetteer shows how long this work could remain useful. Its consulting editor identifies Senapati as Chief Editor and Nabin Kumar Sahu as State Editor of the 1966 volume. When the district was subsequently divided, preparing a new gazetteer involved more than replacing old statistics: the historical account could not be neatly cut along the new boundaries.

The later editors therefore retained the earlier history, explaining that the movements of the Nandapur kingdom connected places and events across the region. They also drew on the earlier gazetteers for geography, archaeology and accounts of people. Senapati and Sahu’s work had become a foundation another generation could examine and extend.

Senapati’s contribution comes into clearest view through this afterlife of the books. The editor’s name may be passed over when a reader turns directly to a village, a temple or a chapter of history. Yet it marks work that made those searches possible—and remains available for correction, comparison and fresh questions.
